loreJson.text: 缝得还算整齐的皮革帽。挡不了什么，但总比淋雨强。
几张皮革缝在一起的外衣。轻是真轻，防护也就那样。
皮革缝的裤子，膝盖处已经磨薄了。穿着倒是很自在。
要走远路的话，这双靴子比赤脚强得多。
一环一环扣出来的头盔，谁也说不清它是从哪里来的。
每一环都还扣得紧，这样完好的锁甲不多见了。
侧面缺了一片环，用铁丝勉强连着。它还是能挡一下的。
几百个铁环连成的胸甲，重量比看起来轻得多。
环与环之间没有一处松动，穿上身几乎没有声音。
背后脱了一大片环，走起路来哗啦作响。前面还是好的。
锁甲的护腿，活动起来比铁的要灵活不少。
每一环都还灵活，弯腿的时候不会卡住。
膝弯处的环断了不少，蹲下去的时候有点勉强。它还是能护住腿的。
用锁甲做的靴子，走在石头上会响。
靴底的环还平整，走起路来不硌脚。
靴底的环磨平了几处，踩到尖石头上会有感觉。脚背那面还是好的。
铁片敲出来的头盔，边缘还有些毛糙。
内衬换过新的，戴上去一点不晃——这样的铁盔并不多。
左边有一处明显的凹痕。前任主人大概不太想谈这件事。
铁片一片片铆起来的胸甲，接缝处还留着锤痕。
胸口錾着一道已经看不清的纹章，内衬换过新的。
左肩有一处明显的凹痕，前一位主人挨过不轻的一下。
铁片铆成的护腿，走路的时候会发出一点声音。
关节处留了余量，蹲下和跑动都不受影响。
接缝处锈住了，弯腿的时候要费点力气。铁还是厚铁。
铁皮包成的靴子，沉是沉，但踩到什么都不会疼。
鞋底加过一层新铁，走碎石路很稳。
靴底的铁皮锈薄了几处。它还是比布鞋强得多。
纯金的头盔，戴上很显眼，防护很有限。
金层比寻常厚一倍，猪灵看见大概会多看你两眼。
表面氧化发暗，擦一擦应该还能亮回来。
金子打的胸甲，好看是真的，一碰就凹也是真的。
胸口那层金打得格外厚，在下界算是通行的身份。
正面有一道压痕——金子太软，受不住这样的力。
金护腿，走路会响，声音还挺好听。
每一片金叶都压得很实，动起来是一片连续的光。
有两片金叶翘了起来，再磕一下大概就掉了。剩下的还很亮。
金靴子，踩在石头上声音清脆，磨损也来得清脆。
靴头包了一层厚金，猪灵看见会稍微客气一点。
靴底的金已经磨得见了底色。它还是很亮。
镶着钻石的头盔，分量不轻，但没人会抱怨这一点。
顶饰断了一根，剩下的部分依然光彩照人。
表面布满细密的划痕，钻石的光泽淡了不少。
整片钻石甲拼成的胸甲，压肩，但没人会嫌它重。
胸口的钻石雕成了一枚纹章，这种手艺现在已经见不到了。
甲片边缘磕出了几处白点。它依然能挡下大部分东西。
钻石的护腿，关节处留得很准，跑起来不受影响。
每片甲的边缘都打磨过，走动的时候光是一整条的。
膝部有几道深痕，是硬顶过什么留下的。还能用很久。
镶着钻石的靴子，踩进岩浆里也还能撑一会儿。
靴面刻着细密的花纹，看得出几乎没怎么落过地。
表面全是细划痕，钻石的光泽淡了。防护倒还在。
黑沉沉的头盔，掉进岩浆里也不会化。

rule.customName: 锻造完美的下界合金头盔

loreJson.text: 合金层包覆得毫无缝隙，戴上之后外面几乎听不见声音。

rule.customName: 有裂纹的下界合金头盔

loreJson.text: 升级时温度没控好，侧面留了一道细纹。它还是硬得离谱。
目前能穿在身上最硬的东西。它也比看起来沉得多。

rule.customName: 锻造完美的下界合金胸甲

loreJson.text: 甲片之间的接缝几乎看不出来，整块像是一次铸成的。

rule.customName: 有裂纹的下界合金胸甲

loreJson.text: 左肋有一道细裂纹，是合金层里的一点小失误。防护没有打折。
下界合金的护腿，走路会有点沉，但踩什么都行。

rule.customName: 锻造完美的下界合金护腿

loreJson.text: 关节处的合金厚薄一致，弯腿的时候没有一点阻力。

rule.customName: 有裂纹的下界合金护腿

loreJson.text: 膝弯处有一道细纹，是升级时留下的。它还是很硬。
穿着它踩岩浆块不会有问题，踩别的东西就更没问题了。

rule.customName: 锻造完美的下界合金靴子

loreJson.text: 靴底的合金整块无孔，走在任何地方都不留痕迹。

loreJson.text: 右脚靴面有一道细纹。穿上之后基本感觉不到差别。
一只海龟留下的壳，戴在头上意外地合适。
用犰狳鳞甲拼成的小铠甲。狼穿上之后看起来相当自豪。
自己缝的皮革马铠，防护有限，但至少马不会晒伤。
给马穿的铁甲，覆盖面比人穿的那件还要大一些。
皮带换过新的，扣件也是配套的，跑起来不会晃。
几处接缝锈住了，马跑起来会响。铁还是好铁。
金灿灿的马铠，防护有限，气势很足。
金层压得很厚，阳光下几乎看不清马本身的样子。
表面暗了一层，擦过之后应该还能亮回来。
镶满钻石的马铠。给马穿这个的人显然很有钱。
每片甲都是手工镶的，看得出是为了某个场合做的。
甲片上全是细划痕，钻石还在，只是光泽淡了。
末地船残骸里找到的翅膀，展开的时候还带着一点风。
膜面没有破洞，边缘的骨架也还结实，飞起来安静得惊人。
膜面上有几块颜色不一的补丁。应该...不影响飞行吧？
平平无奇的灰色石头，地下世界最不缺的就是这个。
切成规整方块再垒起来的石头，比圆石整齐得多。
在切石机上一次裁出来的，尺寸分毫不差。
黏土烧成的砖垒起来的方块，壁炉和烟囱的老朋友。
四块红砖抹上砂浆砌成的，砖缝有点宽，但很结实。
锯开的橡木，纹理清楚，是最常见也最好用的建材。
布面上还留着织机的压痕，图案得自己绣。
木板和羊毛拼的床，够一个人睡；放哪儿都行，别挡着门。

A leather cap sewn reasonably straight. It will not stop much, but it beats standing in the rain.
A tunic made from a few hides stitched together. Genuinely light, and the protection is genuinely modest.
Leather trousers, worn thin at the knees. Comfortable, at any rate.
For a long walk, these beat bare feet by a considerable margin.
A helmet linked together ring by ring, and nobody can quite say where it came from.
Every ring still holds tight. Chainmail in this condition is not a common thing.
A patch of rings is missing at the side, held on with wire. It will still turn a blow.
Several hundred iron rings linked into a chestpiece, and far lighter than it looks.
Not one link is loose, so it makes almost no sound at all when worn.
A whole patch has come away at the back and rattles when you walk. The front is still sound.
Chainmail leggings, and considerably more flexible than the iron equivalent.
Every ring still moves freely, so they will not catch when you bend.
Plenty of rings have gone at the knee, which makes crouching an effort. They still guard the leg.
Boots made of chainmail. They ring against stone underfoot.
The rings under the sole are still flat, so nothing digs in.
The sole rings have ground flat in places, and a sharp stone will come through them. The uppers are fine.
An iron helmet beaten out of sheet, with the edges still a little rough.
The lining has been replaced and it does not shift at all on the head — helmets like this are not common.
An obvious dent over the left side. Its last owner would probably rather not discuss it.
A chestplate riveted together from iron plates, with hammer marks still showing along the seams.
A crest is chased into the breast, worn past reading now. The lining has been replaced.
An obvious dent over the left shoulder. Whoever wore this last took a heavy blow.
Leggings riveted from iron sheet, and they make a little noise when you walk.
There is slack left at the joints, so crouching and running are both unaffected.
The seams have rusted stiff, and bending takes some effort. The iron itself is still thick.
Boots wrapped in iron sheet. Heavy, certainly, but nothing underfoot will hurt.
A fresh layer of iron has been added to the sole, and they hold well on loose stone.
The sole plates have rusted thin in places. They are still far better than cloth shoes.
A helmet of solid gold. Very noticeable, and not very protective.
The gold layer is twice the usual thickness. A piglin will probably look at you twice.
The surface has dulled with oxidation. A good rub should bring it back.
A chestplate of gold. It is genuinely handsome, and it genuinely dents at a touch.
The gold over the breast was laid on especially thick, which passes for status in the Nether.
A dent runs across the front — gold is far too soft to take that kind of force.
Golden leggings. They chime when you walk, and it is a pleasant sound.
Every leaf of gold has been pressed down solid, so movement reads as one continuous shine.
Two leaves have lifted at the edge, and another knock will probably take them off. The rest still shines.
Golden boots. They ring crisply on stone, and they wear down just as crisply.
The toes are capped in a heavy layer of gold, which makes piglins slightly more polite.
The gold at the sole has worn through to the base metal. They are still bright.
A helmet set with diamonds. It is heavy, and nobody ever complains about that.
One of the crest fittings has snapped off, and the rest of it still shines beautifully.
Fine scratches cover the surface, and the diamonds have lost a good deal of their lustre.
A chestplate pieced from whole diamond plates. It sits heavy on the shoulders, and nobody minds.
The diamonds across the breast are carved into a crest, and that kind of work is not seen any more.
Pale chips have been knocked into the edges of the plates. It still stops most of what hits it.
Diamond leggings, cut accurately at the joints, so running is not affected.
Every plate edge has been polished, so the light travels along them in one unbroken line.
Deep marks sit at the knees, left by taking something head-on. They will last a long time yet.
Boots set with diamonds, and they hold up for a while even in lava.
Fine patterning is cut across the uppers, and it is clear they barely ever touched the ground.
Fine scratches cover the surface and the diamonds have gone dull. The protection is still there.
A heavy black helmet that will not melt in lava.
The alloy cladding has not one seam in it, and once it is on you can barely hear the outside.
The temperature was not held during the upgrade and a fine crack is left at the side. It is still absurdly hard.
The hardest thing a person can currently wear. It is also far heavier than it looks.
The seams between plates are all but invisible, so the whole reads as a single casting.
A fine crack runs along the left rib, a small failure in the alloy layer. The protection is not reduced.
Netherite leggings. They make walking heavier, and they let you walk through anything.
The alloy runs even through the joints, so there is no resistance at all when you bend.
A fine crack sits at the back of the knee, left over from the upgrade. They are still very hard.
Magma blocks are not a problem in these, and nothing else is either.
The sole alloy is one unbroken piece, so they leave no mark on anything they walk across.
A fine crack runs across the right uppers. Once they are on, you will not notice the difference.
The shell left behind by a turtle, and it fits on a head surprisingly well.
A small suit of armour pieced together from armadillo scutes. The wolf looks extremely pleased with it.
Horse armour stitched together at home. Limited protection, but at least the horse will not sunburn.
Iron armour for a horse, covering rather more ground than the version made for people.
The straps have been replaced and the buckles match, so nothing shifts at a gallop.
Several seams have rusted stiff and the horse will rattle at a run. The iron is still good iron.
Horse armour in gleaming gold. Limited protection, enormous presence.
The gold is pressed on thick, and in sunlight you can barely make out the horse underneath.
The surface has gone a shade duller. A polish should bring it back.
Horse armour set all over with diamonds. Whoever shod this horse had money.
Every plate was set by hand, and it was clearly made for some particular occasion.
Fine scratches cover the plates. The diamonds are all still there, just rather less bright.
Wings taken from the wreck of an End ship. They still carry a little wind when you spread them.
No holes in the membrane and the frame along the edge is still sound. Astonishingly quiet in flight.
Several mismatched patches across the membrane. That should not... affect the flying, right?
Unremarkable grey stone. The underground has an endless supply of it.
Stone cut into regular blocks and stacked. Considerably tidier than cobblestone.
Trimmed in a single pass on a stonecutter, and accurate to within nothing at all.
Fired clay bricks stacked into a block. An old friend of fireplaces and chimneys.
Four bricks mortared together by hand. The joints are a little wide, but it holds firm.
Sawn oak with a clear grain. The most common building material there is, and one of the most useful.

Sweet and tart, and pleasant enough to eat.
Berries that have been stored a long while. Some of them still taste sour.
Berries that have already gone off. I must be out of my mind with hunger to eat these...
Perfectly ordinary bread, and a favourite ration among travellers.
Perfectly ordinary bread, and a favourite ration among travellers.
Hard bread that looks like it has been sitting around for ages. It fights back a little on the way down.
Shook loose from oak leaves. Crisp, and sweet if you are lucky.
Nobody knows whose pocket it spent the last while in, but the skin is certainly clean.
A few obvious bruises — even so, this is still one of the few fruits an adventurer can count on.
Cooked just right. Charred outside, still juicy when you cut into it.
Left on the fire a bit too long. Tough on the teeth, but it does fill you up.
The fat has set into a white layer. There is no telling how many days it has been sitting here.
A carrot wrapped in a thin sheet of gold. Suspiciously sweet.
Twice the gold leaf of an ordinary one. Probably somebody rich packed this as a snack.
Most of the gold leaf has peeled away, and what is left looks a little sorry for itself.
It smells in a way that defies description. When you are starving, it is not the worst option.
Only lightly spoiled. You can even tell which part of the body it came from.
Nothing about it looks like meat any more. The flies seem fond of it, though.
It is still looking at you. Whatever happens next is on you.
The moisture has gone and the venom has concentrated somewhat. The eyeball has shrivelled too.
Preserved in some kind of brine. The venom is weaker, and so is the flavour.
Eight gold ingots went into this apple. The sweetness carries a hint of metal.
The gold leaf is beaten unevenly and the edges curl up a little, but the effort shows.
An old golden apple engraved with an unfamiliar crest. It sits heavy in the hand.
The surface has dulled with oxidation. A good polish should bring it back.
A golden apple shimmering with every colour at once. Supposedly it used to be food for gods.
Not a trace of wear on the sheen, as though somebody put it in this chest yesterday.
The flesh at the bite mark is still glowing. Who takes one bite of this and puts it down?
A standard ingot of even quality, and the basis of most tools there are.
Still hot enough to sting. A burr along the mould edge suggests the metal was poured in a hurry.
An unfamiliar foundry mark is pressed into one side, and the metal is a grade better than usual.
Pitted with rust all over. It needs a good scraping before it goes back in a furnace.
A crystal squeezed together far underground. The edges will cut you, and the lustre is cold and blue.
Still seated in a ring of host rock, knocked straight out of the vein.
Turn it once in the light and you cannot find a single inclusion. Stones like this are uncommon.
A fleck of black impurity sits inside the crystal. The hardness is still there, it just does not look the part.
The only thing a villager considers to be of any value. Its green is warmer than a diamond's.
Faceted to the standard cut, which makes it far easier to sell over a counter than rough stone.
An unpolished stone whose edges still hold the shape of the vein it came from.
A black lump that burns for a long while, and the most common thing you will haul out of a mine.
A shard peeled off a budding amethyst block. Tap it and it gives a very faint ring.
Heavier than diamond to the touch and quite happy to sit in lava. The material does not much respect the rules.
Four scraps and four gold ingots pressed into one. The process is tedious enough to make you question whether it is worth it.
What the Wither leaves on the ground once it falls. It glows on its own, and it is faintly warm to hold.
The core taken out of the Wither's remains. It glares considerably harder than the stories claim.
A blue gem that is permanently damp. Hold it close and you can hear waves a very long way off.
The one you dug up by following a buried treasure map. There is still sand in the box.
Dried salt is crusted over the shell. There is no saying how many years it spent under water.
A blade whittled out of firewood, and it fells trees far faster than bare hands. It goes dull just as quickly.
A pickaxe made of wood, which stretches the word a little. It does still get through stone.
A flattened chip of wood lashed to a stick. Enough for dirt, though stone is out of the question.
A wooden hoe for breaking up farmland, and it loosens after very little use. The ground still needs turning.
A flake knocked into an edge and bound to a wooden haft, and it is considerably heavier than the wooden one. It lasts considerably longer too.
A point knapped out of stone, and it looks every bit as rough as that. It is already enough to get iron ore out of the rock.
A thinned flake for a blade, and it has some real weight behind it. It moves dirt noticeably faster than the wooden one.
An edge struck off a flake, and it turns soil more cleanly than the wooden hoe.
An iron pickaxe you hammered out yourself, with two wraps of cloth on the grip to spare your hands.
An extra layer of iron plated over the head, meant specifically for hard rock.
The point has been ground round, so you will have to put more muscle into the stone.
An axe forged out of iron, and it feels just as natural felling a tree as anything else.
A counterweight added behind the head, which puts considerably more force into the swing.
The edge has curled over, and the haft is darkened all the way through from sweat.
A head beaten out of iron, and it makes a clean sound going into the ground.
An iron binding run all the way round the head, so gravel cannot chip it.
The head has been worn a good deal thinner all round. It does go into the ground more easily now.
A hoe made of iron, so a whole field can be turned without swapping it out halfway through.
A blade of solid gold, bright enough to hurt the eyes. It starts to deform after about two swings.
A pickaxe made of gold, and it does mine quickly. It does break quickly too.
A head of soft gold, which takes very little effort to push into the ground.
A golden hoe, the most conspicuous and shortest-lived implement in any field.
An edge set with diamonds, and a trunk splits open at the first blow.
A point set with diamonds, and there is very little it cannot mine — obsidian included.
Taken out of a trial chamber vault, and there is still no rock dust anywhere on the point.
Two small chips out of the point, and the grip pattern on the haft has been worn smooth.
A head set with diamonds, and digging goes about as fast as bailing water.
A hoe made out of diamonds. There is no argument about how well it works, only about whether it should.
A blade sheathed in alloy, so it can be fished back out of lava.
The alloy cladding closes without a seam anywhere, and the edge does not glint even in the dark.
The temperature was not held properly during the upgrade, so a fine crack was left in the alloy. It still cuts through anything.
A dark, heavy point, and obsidian feels much like dirt through it.
The point was forged as a single piece, and there is no seam to be found on it.
A fine crack sits inside the alloy, a small mistake left over from the upgrade. Mining is not affected at all.
A head sheathed in alloy, so no amount of digging will turn the edge.
The alloy is plated across the face so evenly that soil simply does not stick to it.
A fine crack where the haft meets the head. It is still very solid.
A hoe made of netherite. Fields turned with it stay turned.
The edge is flat enough to see a face in.
A fine crack was left inside the alloy, though it cannot be seen at all while the ground is being turned.
Three plates of iron beaten into a container that holds more than it looks like it should.
A bucket full to the brim. You still have the bucket afterwards.
A bucket of lava that is still moving about. Best not to trip while carrying it.
Freshly drawn milk, and one drink washes away most of the stranger things affecting you.
A bucket holding snow that will not melt. Poured out, it will trap very nearly anything.
A bucket of water and one cod. It is behaving itself for now.
A bucket of water and one salmon, which keeps circling round the inside.
The colours of the fish in here are hard to describe, though they are certainly bright.
The pufferfish in here is holding a puff of air in reserve. Do not tip it out at your own feet.
An axolotl lying along the bottom of the bucket, its gills still moving slowly.
A few dark specks swimming about in the bucket. Given time they turn into something noisy.
A redstone set inside a golden case, with a hand that always points where the sun ought to be.
The needle points at the place where the world was first generated. Useful when you want to go home.
The needle points at the last place you died. Uncomfortable to look at, but it does get your things back.
Two lenses and a copper tube, good for seeing a long way off. Best to hold still while looking through it.
A sheet with nothing drawn on it yet. Once it has been used it starts recording everywhere you go.
The terrain around you is drawn out on the paper, and everything past the edge is still blank.
A knotted loop, tied to an animal at one end and a fence at the other. It works on other things as well.
A blank iron tag. Once a name is written on it, whatever it is used on will never disappear.
A leather saddle that can be fitted to a horse or a pig. It cannot be crafted — it has to be found.
A horn picked up where a goat charged into something. The sound it makes carries a very long way.
A feather, a copper ingot, and a stick. Brushing suspicious sand is the only way to see what is under it.
A carrot dangled from the end of a rod. Pigs will follow it, right up until the carrot is eaten.
A warped fungus dangled from the end of a rod. Striders know exactly what this is.
Two strikes and you have a spark. The least fussy way to start a fire out in the wild.
The steel has been wiped to a shine and catches on the first try.
The edge of the steel has worn smooth, so it takes several strikes before it will throw a spark.
A pole, a length of line, and one hook. Patience supplies the rest.
The reel is oiled and the hooks have been replaced. Clearly a rod that sees regular use.
The line is tied in knots. Untangling it alone will take you the better part of an hour.
For wool, for leaves, for vines. Occasionally for other things as well.
The blades have been honed thin, and they close with almost no resistance.
The pivot has rusted shut, and they shriek every time you open and close them.
An iron sword beaten out by hand. The workmanship varies, but it is easy enough to make.
An iron sword forged with real skill. Clean lines, a keen edge, and a fine companion for any adventurer!
The failed result of one particular forging. The edge curls up slightly. It still works, it just will not last...
A whittled wooden sword, and the grip still has splinters on it. It will crack soon enough, but it beats empty hands.
Good timber, and the edges are pared evenly — a wooden sword like this is not a common thing.
A crack runs clean through the blade. Best not to block too hard with it.
A blade ground into stone. Heavy it may be, but before iron it was the only choice there was.
The flakes were struck off layer by layer, which leaves a keener edge than grinding ever does.
Chunks are missing from the edge, so it is closer to a saw than a sword. It still works.
A sword made of pure gold. Genuinely bright, and genuinely soft.
An iron core wrapped in a layer of gold — good to look at, and rather more durable than solid gold.
The blade is bent at a considerable angle, and straightening it out would very likely snap it.
A diamond blade ground extremely sharp. Reassuring just to hold.
Faded cloth is wound around the grip. Whoever carried it before clearly got a lot of use out of it.
Several obvious chips along the edge. Still serviceable, though every swing makes you wince.
Black and faintly gleaming, and it can be fished back out of lava. This sword does not much care about its surroundings.
The alloy cladding has not a single seam in it, and the edge does not glint even in the dark.
The temperature was not held during the upgrade, and a fine crack is left in the alloy layer. It is still frighteningly sharp.
Absurdly heavy — a missed swing costs you more than a landed one.
Taken out of an ominous vault in a Trial Chamber, and the chisel marks on the head are still fresh.
The striking face is already beaten concave. Its last owner clearly used it on more than monsters.
A weapon taken off a drowned, and far better in the water than on dry land.
All three points are undamaged, and it still flies back to the hand when thrown.
It lay on the seabed too long, and the shaft has grown a whole layer of green. It still throws a long way.
A yew bow with the string drawn none too tight. Reliable enough all the same.
The limbs curl forward at both ends, and it draws with far more weight than an ordinary bow.
The limbs have taken on damp and warped slightly, which costs you a fair bit of range.
Easier on the arms than a bow, at the cost of a slow reload — so the first bolt had better count.
The prod is capped with iron, and the trigger has a short, clean pull.
The string has gone slack and will not carry far even at full draw. Fit a new one and it is a good crossbow again.
A plank and a lump of iron. The first blow it turns has already paid for it.
A crest is painted across the face, past reading now, though most of the paint is still there.
The crack down the middle is held together by iron nails. Not reassuring against a heavy blow, but it is what there is.
The fletching is still even, so it will not wander in flight.
Picked up off a skeleton, tooth marks on the shaft and all. A wipe down and it is good again.
Whatever it hits keeps on glowing. Nothing hides after that.
Warm to hold. Throw it and it leaves a trail of fire behind, your own sleeves included.
A small pocket of held-in wind. Thrown, it will push someone off a cliff — the thrower included.
It will lift you a good way and light up the sky while it does. Best not used near the ground facing a wall.
A packed ball of gunpowder. What colour it bursts into depends entirely on what went into it.
